body:
Daily Newsletter
                We recommend art novels, catalogs, memoirs, and more, plus an artist reflects on her portable studio.
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
            "The History of Narrative Art: Heroes, Myths, the Sacred” at the Lucas Museum features a digital reproduction of the Cave of Altamira. (photo Matt Stromberg/Hyperallergic)
    
        
            Watch out, Brooklyn Public Library — there are approximately five dozen intriguing art books coming out this season I’d love to get my hands on. But today, my fellow editors and I narrowed our list down to 15 forthcoming titles we think you should read this fall. From a catalog on Kent Monkman’s response to a Vermeer painting to essays by Elizabeth Alexander, find your next art book below.More reads for your Labor Day weekend, including Matt Stromberg’s dispatch from the ill-fated Lucas Museum in Los Angeles and a glimpse into Rujuta Rao’s portable, modular studio.—Lakshmi Rivera Amin, associate editor

	
		
			15 Art Books for Your Fall Reading List
		
	
	
		Christine Sun Kim’s archive of deafness in pop culture, Guadalupe Rosales’s East Los Angeles memoir, Kent Monkman’s pulls back the curtain on a Vermeer painting — it’s choose your own adventure in art books this fall. We’ve got far too many novels, catalogs, essay collections, and photography books coming out over the next three months to pick from, but these 15 caught our eye. Read on for a story within a story, an artist’s take on Moby-Dick from our resident Mellville fan, Associate Editor Lisa Yin Zhang, and much more. Happy reading! —Lakshmi Rivera Amin, associate editor
	
	
		Read More
	


                    
                    
                    
                        
                            Nordic Textile Takeover: The Cold StitchOpening September 4 at Scandinavia House, this exhibition, workshop series, and symposium program returns in its third iteration alongside New York Textile Month.
                        
                        
                            Learn more
                        
                    
            NewsExcavation efforts are set to begin within the next two weeks for President Donald Trump’s controversial “Great Triumphal Arch."Los Angeles

I know that political posters tend to fall off the "art show" spectrum, but I'd suggest adding this to the list - "Graphic Resistance: Seven Decades of California Posters for Peace & Justice" curated by the Center for the Study of Political Graphics at the Santa Monica Airport Arts Studios, 3026 Airport Avenue in Santa Monica. Go soon, closes September 7.—Lincoln Cushing on "15 Art Shows to See in Los Angeles This Fall"Hyper LinksAnne Carson muses on the spiritual experience of attending a Rosalía concert — the crossover we didn't know we needed.Novelist Barbara Kingsolver reflects on the wisdom and lessons of poet Wendell Berry, who passed away last week.A day in the life of the US Open’s unsung heroes: the ball crew.From the Archive

title: The Artist Residency That Never Was
description:
Feature
                Abstract Mag invited dozens of artists to participate in a summer residency in Georgia. Then its social
body:
Feature
                Abstract Mag invited dozens of artists to participate in a summer residency in Georgia. Then its social media pages went dark. 
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
        
            "Rocket" (2026) by Syd Sauer, one of many artists who say they were ghosted by Abstract Mag after applying to their advertised residency (image courtesy Syd Sauer)Like hundreds of other visual artists around the world, 25-year-old airbrush painter Syd Sauer Wilson opened their email inbox on Friday, June 5, to what appeared to be the opportunity of a lifetime: an invitation to participate in an artist residency program hosted by Abstract Mag — a popular art-focused social media platform that had over 1 million followers — taking place overseas this summer.The residency promised an all-expenses-paid retreat in the mountainous regions of southern Georgia, where for two weeks in August, 40 visual artists would live in a “historic chateau” and pursue their practices while also exploring the country’s culture and traditions through a series of expeditions and activities. For the emerging artist hungry for any opportunity to create works in a historic environment without having to pay for travel, materials, or accommodations, a residency like this would be a dream come true.This was the case for Wilson, an early-career artist in Los Angeles. They had applied to last year’s residency, hosted in the 18th-century Château De Forbin in Marseille, for a $40 fee after seeing the open call for artists on Abstract Mag’s social media pages. Though Wilson didn’t apply to this year’s residency in Georgia, they received an email in June from a member of the program’s artist selection committee informing them that, after being shortlisted last year, they were personally invited to participate this August.“We look forward to welcoming you to Georgia this summer,” the end of the email obtained by Hyperallergic reads, with a link that directs the artist to submit more information about their availability, travel information, and any materials they will require during the residency.“ I was super, super excited,” Wilson told Hyperallergic. “I dropped down to the ground on my knees, and I was just like, ‘Oh my God.’ Throughout the day, I just kept looking up at the sky and saying, ‘Thank you, thank you, thank you.’ I called my parents, I shared the news with them, I shared the news with my friends.”But the dream began to crumble after Wilson opened social media to find hundreds of artists coming forward online with reports that they had received similar emails also inviting them to Abstract Mag’s Georgia summer residency this year, raising speculation within the art community about the program’s legitimacy.In July, Abstract Mag announced in since-deleted Instagram posts that 40 artists had been accepted. But artists say they were ghosted after the summer residency’s social media pages all went dark.

title: Preserving Ernie Barnes’s Legacy in Paint Tubes
description:
Features
                The late artist and athlete who rendered joyous scenes of Black life, dance, and motion is the subject
body:
Features
                The late artist and athlete who rendered joyous scenes of Black life, dance, and motion is the subject of renewed institutional attention as his daughter, Erin Barnes, works to conserve his studio practice.
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
            Portrait of Ernie Barnes, 1968 (© Ernie Barnes Family Trust, image courtesy the estate of the artist, Andrew Kreps Gallery, New York and Ortuzar, New York)
    
        
            When artist Ernie Barnes died in 2009, his daughter Erin was left to sort through the vestiges of materials the Los Angeles-based painter and professional football player had accumulated over his decades-long art practice.There were canvases, sure, but also paint tubes, brushes, and containers Barnes kept in the garage that he used as his studio to create vibrant, kinetic scenes of Black church gatherings, football games, and nightlife during the Jim Crow era, including his iconic work “The Sugar Shack” (1976), making him one of Southern California’s most beloved artists.For years, Barnes stored her father’s partially squeezed containers of Liquitex, Grumbacher, and Winsor & Newton acrylic paint and thought little about it until about a year ago, when she began to realize the materials were integral to commemorating his legacy. “I realized how much of the physical studio still existed through the paint tubes and brushes, and I felt a responsibility to preserve them as part of a record of his historical practice,” Barnes told Hyperallergic. “These tubes are the physical remnants of his creative process.”Ernie Barnes, "The Sugar Shack" (1976) (© Ernie Barnes Family Trust, courtesy Museum of Fine Arts, Houston)Black figurative painters such as Jacob Lawrence, Amy Sherald, and Kerry James Marshall have been widely celebrated by museums and institutions in the last decade. Barnes isn’t always mentioned in the same breath as other contemporary art stars despite the $15.3 million sale of “The Sugar Shack” in 2022. (Its buyer, energy trader Bill Perkins, told the New York Times that “for certain segments of America, it’s more famous than the ‘Mona Lisa.’”)That could soon change. A major documentary about Barnes’s life, Who is Ernie Barnes, was announced in July, and the Canton Museum of Art in Ohio recently opened a special exhibition celebrating his work, Good Times: The Artistic Journey of Ernie Barnes, on August 18. Some of Barnes’s works will also be on display at the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art, which opens to the public on September 22.Erin Barnes with a photograph of her father and a selection from her project "Legacy of Color" (photo courtesy Erin Barnes) Barnes grew up in Durham, North Carolina, under Jim Crow segregation, learning about art from books and catalogs because museums did not allow Black people to enter them. Encouraged by his mother, he sketched throughout his childhood and attended North Carolina College (now North Carolina Central University) on a football scholarship. Barnes proved to be a gifted athlete in college and was drafted into the NFL, where he played for five seasons. But he never put aside his art and often made pencil or charcoal sketches of other players while he was on the sidelines during a game.“His teammates were in awe of how he could come up with an idea and sketch it right away,” Thaleen Barnes, Ernie’s second wife, told Hyperallergic. “When we went to places, he watched how people walked, their mannerisms, and how they talked. He was interested in their body, their form and movement. Just looking around the world that we lived in was an inspiration for him to sketch.”

title: In Queens, Immigrant Women Sew a Truer Atlas
description:
Feature
                The largely undocumented Latin American women of New York’s “costureros,” or needlework circles, are cre
body:
Feature
                The largely undocumented Latin American women of New York’s “costureros,” or needlework circles, are creating a countermap to archive the stories of their lives.
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
        
            This article is part of a series focusing on underrepresented craft histories, researched and written by the 2025 Craft Archive Fellows, and organized in collaboration with the Center for Craft."The Collective Map of Paths" (2025–ongoing), 50 x 50 inches (photo by and courtesy Andrés Altamirano)How can we delve into the archives of the present? Is it possible to unveil and touch the documents that communities are creating today to record and remember their history, or does understanding only arise with the passage of time? When does an object become an archive?For the past two years, I have been working with two immigrant-led costureros: circles of women from all over Latin America that gather to create textiles together. Located in different community centers in Northwestern Queens in New York City, these spaces have become a safe haven for many undocumented, working-class immigrants who are enduring racial profiling and persecution under the current immigration crackdown. Amid this terror, the intimacy and secrecy of the costurero set a table where gossip and generosity sit side by side with threads and needles.Costurero member at work, featured in Thread of Voice / Un hilo de voz (photo by and courtesy Andrés Altamirano)The first group, BordeAndo, was founded in 2018 as a community engagement initiative of the Queens Museum, though it soon grew beyond the institution to become an independent collective. Its name plays with multiple meanings in Spanish: bordar (to embroider), borde (border or frontier), and the suffix -ando, which evokes movement or walking. Most of its members come from the Ecuadorian highlands (la Sierra), though others are from the Dominican Republic, El Salvador, and Mexico. They range in age from 30 to 83 and have lived in the United States for between 10 and 50 years.Las Comadres Bordadoras was founded in 2021 in the aftermath of the COVID-19 pandemic by two Mexican immigrants, who sought to bring women out of isolation and foster a mutual support network. Their name, also difficult to translate, gestures toward camaraderie and kinship. The comadre refers specifically to women who are, in their words, “a midpoint between friend and family.” The comadres come from Mexico, Cuba, El Salvador, Uruguay, Colombia, Ecuador, and Argentina; range in age from 35 to 75; and have lived in the United States for between two and 30 years. They mostly embroider Mexican cloth napkins, but all forms of needlework are welcome. This costurero calls itself “nomadic” because it has moved around community gardens, public libraries, and schools in the area since its conception. Both circles are intergenerational, international spaces of confluence for transnational, working-class, largely undocumented immigrant women.Last year, BordeAndo and Las Comadres Bordadoras were the protagonists of Thread of Voice / Un hilo de voz at the Queens Museum. The exhibition, which I curated, featured Andrés Altamirano’s photographs of the costurero members along with film by documentarian Eleonora Privitera. The visual narrative and documentation of this project was also done in collaboration with Altamirano.Still from Eleonora Privitera, “Un hilo de voz” (2025), short film (image courtesy Eleonora Privitera)I see these costureros as living archives — as sites where craft traditions converge, and concrete embodied and material practices connect geographies of affect and displacement, like a woman knitting a stitch learned by her grandmother back home or another embroidering a napkin for the altar of a dead loved one whose grave she cannot visit because of her migratory status. “Text” and “textile” share an etymological root — the Latin verb texere — that reveals both that texts are woven and textiles written. In this sense, textiles are texts that we have forgotten how to read, encoded with bodily gestures, storytelling practices, and materialities that could, if safeguarded, be called archives.
                  
                      
                        Feature
                      
                      
                        Craft Archive Fellowship

title: The Pine Trees That Would Not Leave Me
description: Six years ago, on August 4, 2020, a massive explosion at the Port of Beirut killed more than two hundred people, wounded thousands, and d
body:
Six years ago, on August 4, 2020, a massive explosion at the Port of Beirut killed more than two hundred people, wounded thousands, and devastated large parts of the capital. This August, sitting with a friend at a family-run restaurant amid the pine trees of Dhour El Choueir, a mountain town overlooking Beirut, I found myself unable to shake off a painting and a poem I had translated two decades earlier. Lebanese painter Moustafa Farroukh’s watercolor “A Group of Pines in Bekfaya” was painted just a few miles from here in 1936. Born and first trained in Beirut under the painter Habib Serour, Farroukh later studied in Rome and Paris before returning to establish his practice in his native city. Through portraits and idealized landscapes, he offered a vivid vision of Lebanon’s people and terrain. Farroukh became a foundational figure in modern Lebanese painting, his art helping shape a visual language for the country while its political and cultural identity was still taking form under the French Mandate. The painting of the pine grove was seared into my memory when I first saw it in 2003 in a catalog accompanying a Sursock Museum exhibition of Farroukh’s works. (The watercolor was on loan from the private collection of Emile Nasrallah.) Sursock itself later became a victim of the Beirut Port explosion. The blast shattered its stained-glass windows and damaged the historic building as well as dozens of artworks. The museum reopened on May 26, 2023, with five exhibitions, one of them titled Beyond Ruptures. In August 1937, the Armenian poet Vahan Tekeyan was also here in Dhour El Choueir when he wrote the sonnet “To a Lebanese Pine Tree.” I reconnected with the sonnet after returning home. I corrected a few errors in my translation, adjusted the wording and rhythms, and tried to bring the English closer to the movement of Tekeyan’s Armenian. Here is the translation as I read it now, at twice the age I was when I first attempted it, with many more years of witnessing Lebanon from near and far.To a Lebanese Pine TreeBy Vahan TekeyanDhour El Choueir, Lebanon, August 1937Your pain unfolds from the past, O soft-shadowedpine tree… Barely risen from the groundyou have lost your maiden branch, the trace of whichappears on you, dried and jutting, like a severed arm.Then countless others followed it, one after another…Until, once they thought your trunk had grown large enough,they let your upper branches sprout and thicken,and slowly adorn themselves with translucent tresses.And upon them too, how many fresh traces of the saw —all your grandchildren and great-grandchildren, dead too soon,whose open grave you have become beneath the skies…But you do not at all inspire, O green tree of the mountains,with memories of so many victims, any thought of mourning;you ever bring forth new life and sway in joyous mood…A view from a restaurant in Dhour El Choueir (photo Khatchig Mouradian)Born in Constantinople in 1878, Tekeyan came of age in an Armenian literary world that would be shattered during his lifetime. Poet, editor, teacher, and public figure, he belonged to a generation whose intellectual and literary lives cannot be separated from the violence that dispersed Ottoman Armenians across new geographies.By 1937, Lebanon had become one of the epicenters of Armenian revival in the Middle East. Survivors of the Armenian Genocide had reconstituted community life away from their ancestral towns, rebuilding around churches and secular institutions.Tekeyan participated directly in this process of revival. In September 1937, he became the first editor of a new Armenian newspaper in Beirut, Zartonk (“Awakening,” still published today). Tekeyan included “To a Lebanese Pine Tree,” written the previous month in Dhour El Choueir, in the paper’s inaugural issue, nestled among news items ranging from the upcoming parliamentary elections in French Mandate Lebanon and domestic politics in Palestine to the Spanish Civil War and Mussolini’s visit to Germany. For all the Armenian resonances of Tekeyan’s wounded tree, the poem is emphatically Lebanese. Reading it in Lebanon in August 2026, I was struck less by what the pine might stand for than by how closely its contradictions seemed to belong to the country around me. The poem begins with history lodged in the body. “Your pain unfolds from the past,” Tekeyan tells the tree.The first wound appears low on the trunk. The lost branch resembles a human limb, its trace “dried and jutting, like a severed arm.” Before long, the instrument of amputation appears explicitly: the saw.Moustafa Farroukh, "A Displaced Armenian" (1933) (via Wikimedia Commons)The mutilations accumulate. “Then countless others followed it, one after another.” Yet the tree continues upward. Its higher branches are eventually allowed to sprout and thicken, adorning themselves with “translucent tresses.” Tekeyan lets us glimpse flourishing before making us look again: those branches, too, bear “fresh traces of the saw.”And then Tekeyan shifts the metaphor. The injured body becomes a genealogy. Its branches are its “grandchildren and great-grandchildren, dead too soon.” The ancestor remains standing as its descendants disappear around it.Tekeyan then reverses the natural order of generations: The ancestor becomes the grave of its descendants, “whose open grave you have become beneath the skies.”Everything in the sonnet seems to carry us toward grief.Until it doesn’t.“But you do not at all inspire,” Tekeyan writes, “any thought of mourning.”And he tells us why: “You ever bring forth new life.”In writing and conversation about Lebanon, the word “resilience” is tossed around liberally. But endlessly celebrating people’s resilience can normalize what they are repeatedly forced to endure.No less common in Western media is the portrayal of Lebanon as hedonistic: its nightlife and crowded beach clubs, where the party continues amid economic collapse and political crisis. For decades, such coverage has treated the revival of Beirut’s bars and clubs as evidence that the country is “back.”It is a seductive shorthand. But like the celebration of resilience, this framing romanticizes precarity and escapism while obscuring the scars of war and the uneven costs of crisis. Tekeyan’s pine offers us something more compelling. Farroukh’s pines, in turn, offer a key to reading the poem. Farroukh’s trees stand together. Seen in this light, what is often flattened into hedonism may instead be understood as one manifestation of solidarity: an insistence on gathering with friends and family against the odds, even while bearing the traces of violence.My grandparents were child survivors of the Armenian Genocide who found refuge in Lebanon, where my parents and I were born. I grew up during the Lebanese Civil War and came of age in its aftermath. When I first translated Tekeyan’s poem in 2003 and encountered Farroukh’s painting in the exhibition catalog that same year, I was still living there. Three years later came another war. Soon thereafter, I moved to the United States.But it was only in Dhour El Choueir, in August 2026, that the poem and the painting came together for me, revealing something about Lebanon beyond the familiar scripts.The wounds remain. The tree sways.Acknowledgment: The author would like to thank Rowina Bou Harb, Head of Archives at the Sursock Museum, for her assistance.
                  
                      
                        Opinion
                      
                      
                        Lebanon

title: 15 Museum Exhibitions to See Across the US This Fall
description:
Guide
                Tony Cokes’s riffs on the video essay, a Grandma Moses retrospective, and Abbas Akhavan’s US museum debut
body:
Guide
                Tony Cokes’s riffs on the video essay, a Grandma Moses retrospective, and Abbas Akhavan’s US museum debut are among the shows to look forward to this season. 
                
        
            Grandma Moses, “Halloween” (1955) (© Grandma Moses Properties Co., NY; image via Smithsonian American Art Museum)
    
        
            The circus is coming to town, although maybe not in the form you’d expect. The art world, in all its acrobatics, pageantry, and occasional fun, is returning to cities across the United States this fall with a spate of acts. Artist Karon Davis ushers us into the big top in an exhibition rife with circus archetypes at the Seattle Art Museum. In a group show at the Nasher Museum of Art at Duke University, we’re given front seats to the circus that is American democracy. There may be no ringmaster inside this tent, but there’s certainly showbiz: the Denver Art Museum has dedicated an entire show to the diva phenomenon, while at Virginia Commonwealth University’s Institute for Contemporary Art, Tony Cokes takes the shears to the codes of popular culture. The magic act continues elsewhere: every piece of rubbish that jewelry designer Bernhard Schobinger touched turned into gold, as evidenced by a new show at the Museum of Fine Arts Houston. And up north, a photography exhibition at the Milwaukee Museum of Art pairs the alchemy of resource extraction with that of photography, a comparison that needs no smoke and mirrors, save for the one in a DSLR camera. — Phillip Pyle, associate editor Read our 2026 fall guides for New York and Los Angeles. 
Turn the volume up! Nasher Museum of Art, Duke University, Durham, North Carolina Aug. 27–July 11, 2027Carrie Mae Weems, “Ode to Affirmative Action” (1989) (© Carrie Mae Weems; courtesy the artist and Jack Shainman Gallery, New York)The allusion to NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s celebratory quoting of rapper KRS-One’s “Turn the Volume Up” (2020) in this exhibition’s title is fitting considering its interrogation of democratic participation. Works by artists including Kara Walker, Lyle Ashton Harris, Mike Kelley, and Sam Durant are presented as chronicles of the history of collective action through voting and organizing, inspiring a rare moment of hope amid America’s 250th anniversary.Going Underground: The Jewels of Bernhard SchobingerMuseum of Fine Arts Houston, Houston, TexasSept. 3–Jan. 3, 2027Bernhard Schobinger, “Small Tear Drop Chain” (2014) (photo courtesy Museum of Fine Arts Houston)Fishing lures from Lake Zurich and asphalt chunks from a New York City street are among the materials found in Schobinger’s idiosyncratic jewelry pieces. With influences extending from Concrete Art, Dada, and the Situationists to Japanese culture and punk, Schobinger disrupts jewelry as an elitist luxury through his scavenged, rebellious, and rubbish-composed innovations.Joe Feddersen: Earth, Water, Sky Missoula Art Museum, Missoula, MontanaSept. 4–Dec. 31Joe Feddersen, “Elk at Spotted Lake” (2016) (image courtesy Missoula Art Museum)How do we treat the natural world? Colville artist Joe Feddersen explores the tension in that existential question through decorated woven baskets, spray-painted monoprint collages, and sandblasted blown glass works marked with indigenous symbolisms. This exhibition probes the complex and fragile bond between humans and the environment across four decades of Feddersen's multimedia practice.
Grandma Moses: A Good Day’s Work Crystal Bridges Museum of Art, Bentonville, ArkansasSept. 12–March 29, 2027Grandma Moses, “Black Horses” (1942) (© Grandma Moses Properties Co., NY; courtesy Crystal Bridges Museum of American Art)You can almost hear the festive clamor of the townsfolk in “Deep Snow” (1957), one of the many intimate depictions of rural life in Anna Mary Robertson “Grandma” Moses’s oeuvre. Paintings of farmers knee-deep in hay, green patchwork expanses, and a barnyard wedding (before it became a trend) are part of this major show reviving the postwar legacy of Grandma Moses, who opened her first solo exhibition at 80 years old.The Gift: Emma Amos with Friends Cleveland Museum of Art, Cleveland, OhioSept. 13–Jan. 24, 2027Emma Amos, The Gift (1990–94); top (left to right): India Amos, Grace Williams, Kay WalkingStick; bottom: Lorna Simpson, Joan Semmel, Elizabeth Catlett (© Emma Amos; courtesy Ryan Lee Gallery, New York)As a gift for her daughter India’s 20th birthday, artist Emma Amos painted 48 watercolor portraits of women artists, art historians, and critics in her community. This exhibition brings together the entire suite of paintings in The Gift (1990–94), which includes portraits of Elizabeth Catlett, Lorna Simpson, bell hooks, Faith Ringgold, Howardena Pindell, Lucy Lippard, and Kay WalkingStick, for the first time in two decades. Tony Cokes: Texts, Tracks, Talks (1992–2026)Institute for Contemporary Art, Virginia Commonwealth University, Richmond, VirginiaSept. 18–Feb. 21, 2027Tony Cokes, still from ”Untitled (m.j.: the symptom)” (2020) (artwork © Tony Cokes; image courtesy the artist; Greene Naftali, New York; Felix Gaudlitz, Vienna; Hannah Hoffman, Los Angeles, and Beverly Hills)Tony Cokes’s confrontational text-based, sensory-driven practice samples moments, fragments, and movements across culture and history, spurring new and critical connections that diverge from dominant media narratives. Marking a welcome return to his alma mater, this exhibition presents a survey of the multimedia artist’s existing works alongside newly commissioned ones centering on themes of production, artistic intent, and the development of personal identity. 
From Noguchi to Asawa: Designing Postwar AmericaBarnes Foundation, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania Sept. 20–Jan. 10, 2027Isamu Noguchi, “My Arizona” (1943) (photo courtesy Isamu Noguchi Foundation and Garden Museum, New York)Isamu Noguchi and George Nakashima are among the six Japanese American artists featured in this exhibition that reconsiders the aesthetics of modern America. From album covers to living room lamps, the objects on display illuminate the influence of the artists’ practices in galleries and later, in American homes, where even the most quiet designs were informed by the traumas of World War II and Japanese-American concentration camps in the United States. Martin Puryear: NexusHigh Museum, Atlanta, GeorgiaSept. 25–Jan. 17, 2027Martin Puryear, “Bower” (1980) (© Martin Puryear; courtesy Matthew Marks Gallery, Smithsonian American Art Museum, and Art Resource, New York)This touring exhibition maps the conceptual evolution of Puryear’s contemplative, craft-driven sculpture practice over the last 60 years. Alongside a selection of new works, the artist’s most recognizable pieces are supplemented with rarely seen drawings, prints, and sculptures that nod to his fastidious research and lifelong curiosity. Suzanne Jackson: What Is LoveMuseum of Fine Arts Boston, Boston, MassachusettsSept. 26–Jan. 18, 2027Suzanne Jackson, “Wind and Water” (1975) (© Suzanne Jackson; photo Ruben Diaz, courtesy Ortuzar, New York; Museum of Fine Arts, Boston)From ethereal acrylic washes from the 1970s to a hanging patchwork sculpture from 2017, this retrospective spans Jackson’s career as a painter, dancer, poet, and admirer of the Californian landscape. Infusing her art with luminous imagery and daring abstraction, Jackson positions beauty as political, surrealism as material, and Black artists’ right to make peaceful art as inviolable. Wilmer Wilson IV: SKIRL!Institute for Contemporary Art, University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia, PennsylvaniaSept. 26–Feb. 21, 2027Wilmer Wilson IV, “Untitled” (2025) (image courtesy the artist and ICA Philadelphia)The cheeky, nutty, tenacious, and ubiquitous eastern gray squirrel gets its long-overdue spotlight in Wilmer Wilson IV’s new series of installations, sculptures, performances, and works on paper. As the product of the inaugural edition of the museum’s new research-driven residency, Wilmer’s project examines the social, civic, and cultural relevance of the species whose identity ping-pongs between pest, pet, and wildlife.
DIVA Denver Art Museum, Denver, ColoradoOct. 4–Jan. 31, 2027David Corio, "Whitney Houston performing at Wembley Arena" (1988) (© David Corio; courtesy Denver Art Museum)What drives star power? DIVA answers this by mapping the on- and offstage expectations of performing virtuosas across nearly 150 years of entertainment and fashion history. Honoring the goddesses of opera and silent film, the sex symbols of Hollywood’s Golden Age, jazz and soul icons, and the various iterations of the modern pop star, this exhibition explores the social currency and radical impact of stardom.Fighting for Freedom: Black Craftspeople and the Pursuit of IndependenceGibbes Museum of Art, Charleston, South CarolinaOct. 16, 2026–May 9, 2027David Drake, “Jar” (1861) (photo courtesy Gibbes Museum of Art, Daughters of the American Revolution Museum)This exhibition examines Black craftwork from the Revolutionary War through the present, identifying how the resilience, agency, and personal expression of African American artisans were integral to the route to freedom. These artifacts and design objects, which demonstrate mastery in smithing, carpentry, weaving, and pottery, also shed light on Black communities’ critical contributions to the material culture of the United States. Beneath the Surface: Mining and American PhotographyMilwaukee Art Museum, Milwaukee, WisconsinOct. 23–Jan. 18, 2027 Edward Weston, “Gulf Oil–Pt. Arthur” (1941) (© 1981 Center for Creative Photography, Arizona Board of Regents; courtesy Milwaukee Art Museum)If you drive a car, have a cellphone, use a camera, or own a single piece of plastic, this exhibition is for you. Beneath the Surface juxtaposes the history of American mining, drilling, and fracking with the evolution of photography over nearly two centuries, tracing the social, economic, material, and political evolution of the polarizing industry taking place beneath our feet. Karon Davis: Not My Circus Seattle Art Museum, Seattle, WashingtonNov. 5–July 4, 2027Installation view of Karon Davis's “Human Porcupine” (2021) (© Karon Davis; photo courtesy Wilding Cran Gallery, Los Angeles)In this exhibition themed around the big top, Karon Davis introduces carnivalesque tableaux made from plaster-cast sculptures modeled on those most familiar to her, including herself. As the specters of circuses past haunt today’s oft-empty or repurposed tents, Davis’s subjects carry an unnerving energy, with a despairing clown and a vulnerable knife-thrower's assistant creating an insidious tango between the lighthearted and bleak aspects of performance. Abbas Akhavan: Variations on a GardenWalker Art Center, Minneapolis, MinnesotaNov. 12–April 18, 2027Abbas Akhavan, “curtain call, variations on a folly” (2021/23) (photo David Stjernholm, courtesy the artist and Walker Art Center)Abbas Akhavan’s ephemeral installations probe various conflicts between humans and the natural world through lenses of privacy and preservation. As the first United States museum survey of the Iranian-Canadian artist who represented Canada during the 61st Venice Biennale, this exhibition highlights Akhavan’s use of soil, fauna, and water to emphasize humanity’s role in negotiating the ceaseless and sometimes indifferent forces of biology. 
                  
                      
                        Guide
                      
                      
                        United States

body:
An Yves Saint Laurent Piet Mondrian dress from the 1960s that’s been photographed by the likes of David Bailey, Irving Penn, and Richard Avedon is going under the hammer at the online auction house Fair Warning, in collaboration with Kerry Taylor Auctions. Titled “The Impossible Couture Collection,” the sale also features pieces by Azzedine Alaïa, Elsa Schiaparelli, Paco Rabanne, and John Galliano.

	The sale will take place on the evening of September 17, the first day of London Fashion Week. The auction has been curated by art collector Peter Brant Jr., who is the son of art collector and publisher Peter M. Brant and supermodel Stephanie Seymour. Jussi Pylkkänen, formerly the global president of Christie’s, will auctioneer the sale. 
	

	
		Related Articles
	


	With a presale estimate between $200,000–$500,000, the YSL Mondrian dress is expected to be the top lot of the evening. “It has been decades since a Mondrian Dress of this significance has appeared at auction, making this an exceptionally rare opportunity to acquire one of the defining objects of twentieth-century fashion,” press statement reads.

	Also on offer will be a gold insect collar necklace (estimate: $15,000–$30,000) designed by Elsa Schiaparelli and a custom dress ($600,000–$1 million) from designer Lee Alexander McQueen’s last collection, which was worn by Naomi Campbell.

	Despite the controversy surrounding Galliano’s canceled retrospective at the Metropolitan Museum of Art’s Costume Institute, the auction will still include five gowns and one drawing by the designer, as well as three jewelry pieces he made while serving as creative director of Dior, prior to his firing from the house after making antisemitic comments in 2010; he was convicted of a hate crime in France in 2011. (Galliano decided not to withdraw from the exhibition because of his past remarks.) 

	The priciest Galliano lot comes from his spring 1995 collection, titled “Misia Diva.” Madonna wore the black gown in the music video for “Take a Bow” music video, and Kylie Jenner donned it in 2025 at the 78th British Academy Film Awards. 

	Brant told Vanity Fair in an interview that he was “certainly disappointed” about the cancelation of Galliano’s exhibition, adding, “We were hoping that we would see some of these dresses on the red carpet.”

schema.headline: Fair Warning to Auction Rare Yves Saint Laurent Mondrian Dress and Several Pieces by John Galliano Despite Controversy over Met Museum Exhibition’s Cancellation
